description:
¿Y si la clave para conquistar otros mundos ya estuviera en la Tierra?
Nuestro equipo busca cerrar la brecha entre la exploración terrestre y la espacial. Aprovechando los datos abiertos de la NASA, estamos construyendo una solución innovadora para detectar regiones terrestres análogas a Marte y la luna. Queremos transformar información compleja en un mapa accesible que impulse el futuro de la ciencia planetaria y la exploración humana.
summary:
TERRA-TWIN // Planetary Analog Explorer is a web application for identifying and evaluating new terrestrial analogs for future lunar bases and landing sites on Mars. It compares nine understudied sites on Earth with real destinations, including the Artemis III region near the lunar South Pole and Gale, Jezero, and Gusev craters on Mars.

The tool goes beyond visual resemblance. For each pair, it explains what is similar, how closely the sites match, and where the analogy breaks down. Its similarity index combines geology, topography, temperature, subsurface conditions, and dust, drawing on live, open data from NASA POWER, Moon and Mars Trek, and ESA Copernicus. Additional features include a traffic-light indicator of evidence quality, study parcels mapped at their true scale on both worlds, calibration against established analog sites, and a reverse-search tool for identifying candidate areas.

TERRA-TWIN helps teams select test sites quickly, transparently, and verifiably. This can reduce the cost of testing rovers and habitats ahead of Artemis missions and future missions to Mars.
details:
TERRA-TWIN // Planetary Analog Explorer is a web application that helps identify and evaluate new terrestrial analogs for future lunar bases and landing sites on Mars. It goes beyond visual resemblance. For each Earth–destination pair, it answers three questions: what is similar, how closely the sites match, and where the analogy breaks down.

What it does and how it works

The application compares nine understudied sites on Earth with specific destinations on the Moon and Mars, including a ridge within a candidate Artemis III landing region near the lunar South Pole and Gale, Jezero, and Gusev craters on Mars.

Each pair receives a similarity score from 0 to 100 across five dimensions: geology, topography, thermal extremes, subsurface conditions, and dust/aeolian processes. Topographic and climate metrics are calculated from data retrieved live: slope comes from a transect of the Copernicus Digital Elevation Model (DEM), while climate metrics come from NASA POWER climatology.

A traffic-light indicator identifies the evidence behind each value: green for metrics calculated from live data retrieval, yellow for values from cited literature, and gray for assumptions awaiting verification.

The tool is organized into three stations:

  1. Dual maps: A 3 × 1.5 km study parcel is displayed at its true geographic scale on Earth and at the destination, alongside the landing ellipse of an actual mission—Curiosity, Perseverance, InSight, or Spirit—or a 15 × 15 km Artemis III region.
  2. Rover route planning: An A* pathfinding algorithm operates on a slope grid, supported by an energy model that accounts for the destination’s gravity and a 3D route viewer.
  3. NASA POWER data, comparative analysis, and calibration: The same data-derived similarity index is applied to established analog sites—Atacama, Haughton, Mauna Kea, Death Valley, and the Antarctic Dry Valleys—to benchmark each proposed site. These reference sites serve exclusively as controls and are never presented as new candidates.

Additional features include:

  • A reverse-search tool that combines regional NASA POWER climate data with DEM-derived slopes to suggest new candidate areas, always labeled “requires verification.”
  • A free-click mode for evaluating any location on Earth.
  • A four-step guided tour introducing each site.
  • A downloadable team report covering the methodology, ranking, limitations, and sources.

Benefits

Teams developing rovers, habitats, and experiments gain a fast, transparent, and reproducible way to shortlist terrestrial test sites.

Each pair includes a proposed experiment specifying what to measure, which instrument to use, a concrete success criterion—for example, wheel slip below 20% on basaltic scoria at slopes of 10–15°—and the intended users. The tool also identifies each site’s relevance to water or ice exploration and astrobiology.

Expected impact

We aim to expand the range of analog sites beyond the usual locations, reduce field-testing costs ahead of Artemis and Mars missions, and set a higher standard for transparency: explaining where an analog falls short—in gravity, vacuum, radiation, or regolith chemistry—as clearly as where it is useful.

Tools and technologies

The application runs from a single HTML file built with JavaScript, React 18, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for mapping, and Three.js for 3D visualization. It requires no specialized hardware and works on computers and mobile phones with an internet connection.

It uses the following open data sources:

  • NASA: POWER for climate data; Moon Trek and Mars Trek for LRO WAC imagery, LOLA elevation data, Diviner thermal data, lunar South Pole NAC mosaics and permanently shadowed regions, MGS MOLA elevation data, and Viking imagery; and GIBS/Worldview for MODIS imagery.
  • Partner agencies: ESA/Copernicus resources, including Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery and the Copernicus DEM.

Creativity

TERRA-TWIN brings together three capabilities that are often separate: scientific comparison, mission engineering through rover route and energy modeling, and visualization of study areas at their true scale across planetary bodies.

It proposes new pairings, such as a polar desert plateau in Greenland for practicing operations under low-angle sunlight and excavating ice-bearing ground, with the lunar South Pole in mind.

The reverse-search tool also changes the starting point: instead of beginning with a familiar location, it searches Earth for areas that match a target climate and slope profile.

Design considerations

  • Traceability: Every data value has an identifiable source.
  • Transparency about novelty: Previously studied sites are labeled “known site, new study parcel and application.”
  • Evidence clarity: Data-derived metrics, cited findings, and assumptions remain clearly distinguished.
  • Physical limitations: Each analogy explicitly states its limitations.
  • Accessibility: The application runs in a browser, supports mobile devices, and is available in Spanish.
  • Practical usefulness: Every site leads to an experiment with verifiable outcomes.
